d.title: Setting the derivative to zero gives covariance over variance
d.caption: Two unknowns, two equations, one line of algebra each. The second equation is the one worth remembering: the fitted line passes through the **centroid** of the data, which is why centring the features makes the intercept equal the mean of y.

d.title: The same estimate as a projection
d.caption: Least squares projects y onto the column space of X. The residual is **orthogonal** to every column, which is the geometric statement of the normal equation — and it is why adding any column can never increase the residual, hence why R² never falls when you add a feature, useful or not.

d.title: Four derivations of one estimate, and what each is for
d.caption: They give the same β-hat and answer different questions. An interviewer asking 'derive it' wants the second; 'why squared error' wants the fourth; 'why does that one point move the line so much' wants the third. Knowing which view answers which question is most of what fluency here means.

d.title: Five ways to solve it, and when each breaks
d.caption: The normal equation squares the condition number, so it is the first to fail under collinearity — which is why `LinearRegression` does not use it. QR/SVD is the default because it handles rank deficiency by returning the minimum-norm solution instead of raising.

d.title: The same machinery, on a table with a kink in it
d.caption: Spend accrues at fee × months for the first twelve months and then flattens — so a single slope in tenure cannot fit both halves, and the diagnostics of 4.2 say so loudly. The fix is not a different algorithm: it is the interaction term the data's own structure implies.

nodes.label: Fit a line in tenure

d.title: Six assumptions, and what breaks when each one fails
d.caption: Only two of the six threaten the coefficients themselves; three threaten the **standard errors**, which is why a p-value is only as honest as the assumptions behind it. The last cannot be tested from the data at all — an omitted confounder leaves no residual signature, which is the whole reason causal claims need a design.

cells.text: SEs too small, p too good

d.title: The diagnostics on the real model, band by band
d.caption: Two failures, both visible in the same table. The **mean** residual bends: a straight line under-predicts new customers by £56 and over-predicts one-year customers by £28, and the RESET test rejects linearity at p = 1e−5. The residual **sd** falls from 36.7 to 9.4 — thirteen times the variance at the start of tenure — and Breusch-Pagan rejects equal variance at p = 6e−44. The cause is one fact about the data: spend accrues at fee × months for the first twelve months.

d.title: Leverage, outlier, influence — three different things
d.caption: A point can be extreme in x and sit exactly on the line, contributing nothing; or be moderate in x with a large residual and barely move the fit. Influence is the product of the two, which is why Cook's distance is the statistic to read and not either input on its own.

d.title: When the standard error is wrong, fix the standard error
d.caption: Heteroscedasticity and correlated errors leave the coefficients unbiased and make their standard errors wrong — so the repair is to the **uncertainty**, not the fit. Robust and clustered errors make no distributional claim at all; they estimate the variance from the residuals you actually got.

nodes.label: Weighted least squares
nodes.sub: if you can model the variance

d.title: Ridge in the SVD basis: it shrinks the weak direction hardest
d.caption: The data has two directions carrying d² = 22.68 and 2.12 of variance. Ridge multiplies each direction's coefficient by d²/(d²+λ), so at λ = 1 the strong direction keeps **96%** and the weak one **68%**; at λ = 10 the weak direction is mostly gone. That is the whole mechanism: ridge does not shrink every coefficient equally, it shrinks in proportion to how little the data says about that direction.

d.title: Lasso by soft-thresholding, worked to convergence
d.caption: Coordinate descent updates one coefficient at a time with the soft-threshold S(ρ, λ) = sign(ρ)·max(|ρ| − λ, 0). With ρ₀ = 6.325, each λ subtracts itself from the correlation — and at λ = 5 the subtraction leaves 1.325, which after cycling drives feature 0 to **exactly zero**. The hand calculation matches scikit-learn to three decimals.

d.title: Why L1 lands on the corner and L2 never does
d.caption: The constraint region's shape decides it. A diamond has corners **on the axes**, and a contour of the squared error is overwhelmingly likely to first touch a convex region at a corner; a circle has no corners, so the solution is shrunk but never exactly zero. The prior view says the same thing: a Laplace prior has a spike at zero, a Gaussian does not.

d.title: Correlated features are where the three penalties part company
d.caption: This is the practical reason to prefer elastic net when you do not know the structure: with a correlated group, ridge shares the weight and stays stable, lasso picks one member **arbitrarily** — so a resample can change which one — and elastic net keeps them together.

d.title: The degree sweep, all the way to catastrophe
d.caption: Read the training column: it falls monotonically from 0.559 to **0.062**, the whole way, and never once warns you. The test column bottoms at degree 5 — at 0.102, just above the noise floor of 0.09 — then climbs to **728.893** at degree 20. Cross-validation sounds the alarm first, exploding at degree 12 while the single test split still looks acceptable, because a fold that extrapolates slightly past its training range is enough to wreck a degree-12 polynomial. And the last column explains all of it: the largest coefficient goes from 0.58 to **1,910**.

d.title: Why a high-degree polynomial fails twice over
d.caption: Two separate failures that arrive together. The statistical one is variance — oscillation between the points. The numerical one is conditioning: the columns x, x², x³ ... are nearly collinear, so the Vandermonde matrix's condition number explodes and the coefficients are solved unreliably even where the fit is fine.

d.title: Which dial to turn, by the shape you need
d.caption: A global polynomial cannot make a corner — it pays for one with oscillation everywhere else. Splines put the flexibility where the knots are and leave the rest alone, which is why they are the default for one smooth input. With many inputs, do not expand at all: let a tree ensemble find the interactions and engineer the two or three it points at.

d.title: From odds to the sigmoid, in one line of algebra
d.caption: The sigmoid is not chosen for its shape — it is what you get by asserting that the **log-odds** are linear and then solving for p. That is why logistic regression's coefficients are read as log-odds, and why exponentiating one gives an odds ratio rather than a probability change.

items.label: Model the log-odds as linear
items.desc: log(p / (1 - p)) = Xb — the assumption, stated

items.label: That is the sigmoid
items.desc: derived, not assumed; bounded in (0, 1) by construction

items.label: So a coefficient is a log-odds change
items.desc: and exp(coefficient) is an odds ratio, not a probability

d.title: The gradient that falls out of the likelihood
d.caption: Write the Bernoulli likelihood, take its negative log, differentiate — and the sigmoid's derivative cancels the log's, leaving **X'(p − y)**: the features weighted by the residual, with no second-order term in sight. The same form appears in linear regression with p replaced by the prediction, which is why both fit with the same optimiser.

d.title: The sign that flipped: fee and plan in the same model
d.caption: The fee is 7.99, 12.99 or 19.99 **by plan**, plus half a pound of noise — so fee and the plan dummies are nearly the same information. VIF is 77 for fee and 84 for plan_pro. The pair's joint effect is estimated fine; its split between them is arbitrary. Check VIF before reading an odds ratio.

d.title: Sweeping C, and the separation that has no finite answer
d.caption: On 863 rows with 11 columns the penalty barely matters — log-loss moves from 0.3726 to 0.3757 across five decades of C, because there is little variance to remove. Tune it anyway; it costs nothing. The second block is the pathology: with **perfectly separable** data the likelihood keeps improving as the coefficient grows, so the unpenalised MLE does not exist — the coefficient went 2.67 to 15.11 and the training loss to 0.0544 on its way to infinity. Any penalty at all makes the problem well-posed.

d.title: One model, three components
d.caption: Every GLM is these three choices, and naming them separately is what makes the family comprehensible. The **random** component says how the spread grows with the mean; the **link** says on what scale the effects add up; the linear predictor is the part that looks like ordinary regression.

children.label: Random component
children.sub: the distribution: Normal, Poisson, Gamma, Tweedie

d.title: IRLS: a GLM is weighted least squares, solved repeatedly
d.caption: There is no closed form, but there is something almost as good: linearise the link around the current fit, compute a working response and a weight per row, and solve an ordinary weighted least squares. Iterate and it converges — usually in four or five passes — which is why GLMs were practical decades before general optimisers were.

d.title: Overdispersion: the coefficient is fine and the standard error is a lie
d.caption: The sample's variance is 3.989 against a mean of 1.837 — Poisson requires them equal, and φ = 1.77 measures the gap. Every method below recovers β₁ ≈ 0.382 correctly; they differ only in the **standard error**, and Poisson's is too small by a factor of √1.77. The consequence is measurable: across 200 simulations the nominal 95% Poisson interval contained the truth **79.5%** of the time — one interval in five is wrong — against 93.0% for quasi-Poisson.

d.title: Choosing the loss is choosing a likelihood
d.caption: Squared error is the Normal likelihood and absolute error is the Laplace — so 'change the loss' and 'change the family' are the same move seen from two sides. Huber caps the gradient, which is exactly what makes contamination unable to drag the fit.
